---
title: "The MLSys·im Philosophy"
subtitle: "First-Principles Analytical Modeling with Sourced Numbers"
---

MLSys·im was built to solve a specific problem in machine learning systems education and engineering: **the gap between abstract intuition and cycle-accurate simulation.**

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Hardware, Models, Systems

_a100 = Hardware.Cloud.A100
_h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
_l2_70 = Models.Language.Llama2_70B

_a100_peak = _a100.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
_a100_bw = _a100.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude
_a100_ridge = (_a100.compute.peak_flops / _a100.memory.bandwidth).to("flop/byte").magnitude

_h100_peak = _h100.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
_h100_bw = _h100.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude
_h100_ridge = (_h100.compute.peak_flops / _h100.memory.bandwidth).to("flop/byte").magnitude

_flops_ratio = (_h100.compute.peak_flops / _a100.compute.peak_flops).to("dimensionless").magnitude
_bw_ratio = (_h100.memory.bandwidth / _a100.memory.bandwidth).to("dimensionless").magnitude

_l2_70_wt_gb = _l2_70.size_in_bytes("fp16").to("GB").magnitude
_ib_ndr_gbps = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth.to("Gbps").magnitude
_mega_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Mega_100K.total_accelerators
_train_10k_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators
```

When reasoning about ML infrastructure, whether sizing a serving fleet for LLaMA-3 or estimating the carbon footprint of a `{python} f"{_train_10k_gpus:,}"`-GPU training run, engineers often rely on spreadsheets filled with hidden assumptions, unit-conversion errors, and unexplained constants. Conversely, cycle-accurate simulators require weeks of setup, deep proprietary knowledge, and hours to run a single workload.

MLSys·im provides a third path: **First-Principles Analytical Modeling**.

The framework follows four design principles.

---

## 1. Every Number Has a Source

A language model asked to "estimate the latency of ResNet-50 on an A100" will return a number, but it has no source for it and the number is often wrong.

MLSys·im computes every estimate from stated equations and sourced inputs.

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme': 'neutral'}}%%
flowchart LR
    A[<b>Primary Source</b><br/><i>Datasheet / Paper</i>] -->|provenance| B(<b>Registry</b><br/><i>e.g., Hardware.Cloud.H100</i>)
    B -->|Sourced Value<br/>+ SI Units| C{<b>Solver Engine</b>}
    C --> D[<b>Trusted Estimate</b><br/><i>No Unexplained Constants</i>]

    style A fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#cbd5e1
    style B fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#94a3b8
    style C fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0284c7,stroke-width:2px
    style D fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#10b981
```

Every number in the MLSys·im ecosystem is mathematically derived from explicit, vetted constants. If a solver needs the memory bandwidth of an H100 GPU, it does not use a hardcoded float `3000.0`. It queries the `Hardware` registry, which returns a `Sourced` object containing `{python} f"{_h100_bw:.2f} TB/s"`, complete with a `Provenance` struct linking directly to the NVIDIA H100 datasheet.

If a student or engineer asks, *"Where did this number come from?"*, the framework provides the exact URL, the academic paper, or the empirical methodology used to derive it. No unexplained constants are hidden in the source code.

## 2. Dimensional Strictness (SI Units Everywhere)

The most common source of error in back-of-the-envelope systems analysis is unit mismatch (e.g., dividing gigabytes by gigabits per second without a factor of 8).

To physically prevent these errors, MLSys·im enforces **strict dimensional analysis at runtime** using the `pint` unit library.

*   A workload of `{python} f"{_l2_70_wt_gb:.0f} GB"` (Llama-2 70B in FP16) is represented with explicit units (`ureg.GB`), not as a bare number.
*   A network link of `{python} f"{_ib_ndr_gbps:.0f} Gbps"` (InfiniBand NDR) is represented with explicit units (`ureg.Gbps`), not as a bare number.
*   If a user accidentally attempts to add a latency (`ms`) to a throughput (`1/s`), the Python interpreter will instantly raise a `DimensionalityError`.

By forcing every input, intermediate variable, and output to carry physical SI units, the framework rejects any calculation whose units do not match.

## 3. Analytical Speed over Cycle-Accurate Simulation

MLSys·im is an **analytical engine**, not a discrete-event simulator.

We do not track individual packets across a network switch, nor do we simulate warp-scheduler occupancies inside a GPU streaming multiprocessor. Instead, we use closed-form equations (like the Roofline model, the $\alpha$-$\beta$ communication model, and Erlang-C queueing theory) to establish the **hard physical bounds** of a system.

By relying on analytical math ($Y = f(X)$):
*   **Evaluation is instantaneous:** A full-stack analysis of a `{python} f"{_mega_gpus:,}"`-GPU cluster takes less than 0.3 seconds on a standard laptop.
*   **Bottlenecks are explicit:** Closed-form equations make it easy to take gradients (Sensitivity Analysis) or invert an equation to find the required hardware (Synthesis Analysis).
*   **Intuition is preserved:** Analytical models expose *why* a system behaves as it does (e.g., comparing the H100 to the A100 shows that FP16 peak compute rises `{python} f"{_flops_ratio:.1f}"`× from `{python} f"{_a100_peak:.0f}"` to `{python} f"{_h100_peak:.0f} TFLOP/s"` while HBM bandwidth rises `{python} f"{_bw_ratio:.1f}"`× from `{python} f"{_a100_bw:.2f}"` to `{python} f"{_h100_bw:.2f} TB/s"`, shifting the ridge point from `{python} f"{_a100_ridge:.0f}"` to `{python} f"{_h100_ridge:.0f} FLOP/byte"`), whereas detailed simulations only show *that* a workload is slow.

To bridge the gap between theoretical peaks and realized performance, MLSys·im introduces a single, explicit **Efficiency Coefficient ($\eta$)** into compute-bound solvers (such as MFU). This clearly separates the raw physics of the hardware from the software friction of the framework.

## 4. Separation of Demand and Supply

A recurring anti-pattern in systems modeling is tightly coupling a model to the hardware it runs on (e.g., writing a script specifically for "GPT-3 on A100").

MLSys·im enforces a strict **Demand vs. Supply abstraction**:

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme': 'neutral'}}%%
flowchart TB
    subgraph Demand["<b>Demand (Workloads)</b>"]
        direction TB
        W["<i>Transformer / CNN</i><br/>Parameters & FLOPs"]
    end

    subgraph Supply["<b>Supply (Hardware & Systems)</b>"]
        direction TB
        H["<i>Compute & Memory</i><br/>TFLOP/s & Bandwidth"]
    end

    Demand -->|Lower to graph| S["<b>Solvers (Layer E)</b>"]
    Supply -->|Physical Constraints| S
    S --> R["<b>Analytical Prediction</b><br/><i>Latency, Bottleneck, Cost</i>"]

    style Demand fill:#fef08a,stroke:#d97706
    style Supply fill:#ddd6fe,stroke:#7c3aed
    style S fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0284c7,stroke-width:2px
```

*   **Demand (Workloads):** A `TransformerWorkload` only knows about its parameters, sequence length, and arithmetic intensity. It has no concept of what a GPU is.
*   **Supply (Hardware/Systems):** A `HardwareNode` only knows about its peak TFLOP/s, memory hierarchy, and power draw. It has no concept of what a Transformer is.

Demand and supply meet in the **Solvers** (Layer E). A solver takes the abstract Demand, maps it onto the physical Supply, and applies the governing equations to predict the outcome.

Because of this decoupling, a workload defined once can be swept instantly across every hardware device in the `Silicon Zoo`, from a 1-Watt microcontroller to a 100-MegaWatt supercomputer.

---

## Conclusion

MLSys·im is the executable companion to the [Machine Learning Systems](https://mlsysbook.ai) textbook. It replaces informal estimates and ad hoc spreadsheets with a composable tool that checks units and states its equations.

When MLSys·im reports that a system will bottleneck on memory bandwidth, an engineer can trust the math, check the units, and audit the datasheets.
